summary: The novel opens with a stone left over from the goddess Nüwa's repair of the heavens. It asks a Taoist priest and a Buddhist monk to carry it into the world of red dust, and it is reborn as Jia Baoyu, born with a piece of jade in his mouth. The story follows life in the Rongguo and Ningguo houses of the wealthy Jia clan, the young women of the family, the building of the Daguanyuan garden for a royal consort, and the slow decline of the family's fortunes. This site carries Book I of the Joly translation, chapters I to XXIV.
context: Cao Xueqin began the book in the 1740s and worked on it until he died in 1763 or 1764. He left 80 finished chapters, which circulated in hand copies among friends and were then sold. Cheng Weiyuan and Gao E printed the first 120-chapter edition in 1791 and 1792, adding 40 chapters, and it became the most widely read version. The prose is written in vernacular Chinese, not classical. Its Beijing dialect later helped shape modern standard Chinese. The Gutenberg text here is the first of two books in H. Bencraft Joly's English translation.

people.name: Cao Xueqin
people.note: Qing dynasty novelist whose family served the Manchu emperors and then declined.

people.name: Gao E
people.note: Co-editor of the 1791 and 1792 printed editions that added 40 chapters.

places.name: Nanjing
places.note: Cao's family moved to Jiangning, now Nanjing, when his great-grandfather took the textile commissioner post.

places.name: Beijing
places.note: The dialect of the dialogue is Beijing Mandarin, which became the base of modern spoken Chinese.

ideas.title: Rise and fall of a family
ideas.note: The plot follows a great clan from its peak of prestige to decline, much like Cao's own family.

ideas.title: Memorial to women
ideas.note: Cao wrote it as a memorial to the women he knew in his youth: friends, relatives and servants.

ideas.title: The stone and the red dust
ideas.note: A frame story of a sentient stone that wants to experience the mortal world frames religious and philosophical questions.

passages.quote: This translation was suggested not by any pretensions to range myself among the ranks of the body of sinologues, but by the perplexities and difficulties experienced by me as a student in Peking, when, at the completion of the Tzu Erh Chi, I had to plunge in the maze of the Hung Lou Meng
passages.why: The translator explains why he made this version.
